questions.question: What is a Merkle tree?

options.text: A tree of hashes where each non-leaf node is the hash of its children, enabling efficient verification

questions.explanation: Merkle tree: binary tree of hashes. Leaves: hashes of data blocks. Parents: hash of children's hashes. Root: single hash representing all data. Enables efficient verification and sync. Used in Git, Bitcoin, databases.

questions.question: What is the Merkle root?

options.text: The single hash at the top representing all data in the tree

questions.explanation: Merkle root: top hash. If any data changes, its leaf hash changes, propagating up to root. Comparing roots tells you if two datasets are identical. Single hash summarizes entire dataset.

questions.question: How do Merkle trees enable efficient data verification?

options.text: By allowing verification of any piece with O(log n) hashes instead of checking all data

questions.explanation: Merkle proof: to verify one leaf, need only O(log n) hashes (path to root). Don't need entire dataset. Verifier with trusted root can confirm any piece. Efficient for large datasets.

questions.question: How does Bitcoin use Merkle trees?

options.text: To efficiently verify transactions are in a block without downloading all transactions

questions.explanation: Bitcoin: each block has Merkle tree of transactions. Light clients store only block headers (with Merkle root). To verify transaction, request Merkle proof (O(log n) hashes). SPV (Simplified Payment Verification).

questions.question: How does Git use Merkle trees?

options.text: Every commit, tree, and blob is content-addressed by hash, forming a Merkle DAG

questions.explanation: Git: content-addressed storage. Blob hash = hash(content). Tree hash = hash(children). Commit hash = hash(tree + parent + metadata). Merkle DAG (not tree). Enables: integrity verification, deduplication, efficient sync.

questions.question: How do distributed databases use Merkle trees?

options.text: To efficiently detect and sync differences between replicas (anti-entropy)

questions.explanation: Anti-entropy with Merkle trees: each replica builds tree over its data. Compare roots: if equal, in sync. If different, traverse tree to find differing subtrees. Efficiently identify what to sync. Used in Cassandra, DynamoDB.

questions.question: What is a Merkle proof?

options.text: The set of hashes needed to verify a leaf belongs to a tree with a given root

questions.explanation: Merkle proof: sibling hashes along path from leaf to root. Given leaf data and proof, can compute root. If matches trusted root, leaf is authentic. O(log n) proof size. Enables trustless verification.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to verify data integrity using a Merkle tree?

options.text: O(log n)—only need to check path from leaf to root

questions.explanation: Verification: O(log n). Tree height is log n. Verify one leaf: hash leaf, combine with sibling, hash, repeat to root. Compare with trusted root. Much better than O(n) full data comparison.

questions.question: What happens to the Merkle root if one data block changes?

options.text: The root changes because the change propagates up through all ancestor hashes

questions.explanation: Any change propagates: changed block → new leaf hash → new parent hash → ... → new root. This is the key property: root is a fingerprint of entire dataset. Any tampering is detectable.

questions.question: What is the space overhead of a Merkle tree?

options.text: Approximately n-1 additional hashes for n data blocks (roughly doubles hash storage)

questions.explanation: Space: n leaves + (n-1) internal nodes = 2n-1 hashes total. Overhead is O(n) but constant factor ~1x. For 32-byte hashes and 1KB blocks, overhead is ~3%. Worthwhile for verification benefits.

questions.question: What is a Merkle DAG?

options.text: A Directed Acyclic Graph where nodes are content-addressed by hash (like Git)

questions.explanation: Merkle DAG: generalization of Merkle tree. Nodes can have multiple parents (DAG, not tree). Each node addressed by hash of content. Used in: Git (commits have multiple parents), IPFS. Same integrity properties.

questions.question: Two database replicas need to sync efficiently. They have millions of records. Best approach?

options.text: Build Merkle trees, compare roots, traverse to find differences

questions.explanation: Merkle tree sync: compare roots (1 comparison). If different, compare children (2 comparisons), recurse into differing subtrees. Find all differences in O(d * log n) where d is number of differences. Much better than O(n).
